title: Why a cell pays to keep its chemistry apart

objectives.statement: Given a stated cellular job, name the maintained condition it requires before naming any organelle, identify the compartment that holds that condition, and predict the loss of function that follows when the condition alone is removed while every component stays intact.

Compute the ratio of hydrogen-ion concentrations between two compartments from their pH values, compare that result with an independently reported gradient, and state both what the difference costs the cell to hold and what the arithmetic cannot establish.

Predict where a product ends up and what stops working when a named step on the route from gene to working location fails, distinguishing a fault of manufacture from a fault of delivery and locating the failure at the correct step.

scenes.title: A cell with two outsides
scenes.contentHtml:
A cell with two outsides

Pick one absorptive cell near the top of a colonic crypt and stand it up the way it actually sits. Above it is the lumen: water, salts, whatever the bacteria down there have finished fermenting, and the bacteria themselves. Below it is the tissue, the blood supply, and the rest of you. The cell is the join.

Anatomy calls this cell a colonocyte, and it is the absorptive kind of enterocyte that makes up most of the colonic lining. It is polarised, meaning its two ends are built differently and do different work. The end facing the lumen carries microvilli, fine finger-like projections packed so densely that they form a single fuzzy border under a light microscope. A mature absorptive cell of this kind carries around a thousand of them. They multiply the area available for taking things up, and water absorption from the gut contents happens across them. The other end faces neighbouring cells and the sheet of material the epithelium sits on, and it is where the cell hands its cargo onward.

Two names to keep straight, because the rest of the lesson uses them constantly. The lumen-facing end is apical. The other end, along with the sides in contact with neighbours, is basolateral. They are not interchangeable. A pump that belongs on one of them is useless on the other, and a great deal of what this cell does is a matter of getting the right protein to the right face.

The division you cannot see from outside

So far this is a division of the cell's surface. The more interesting division is inside.

If you could open the cell, you would not find one bag of soup with machinery floating in it. You would find membranes running all through the interior, folding into stacks and tubes and closed sacs, marking off spaces that are chemically nothing like the fluid around them. Taken together, those membrane-enclosed compartments occupy close to half the volume of a cell. Each one holds its own distinct set of proteins, which is another way of saying each one does a job the others do not.

That should look expensive, because it is. Membrane costs lipid and protein to build. Anything the cell wants to move from one compartment to another now has to cross a boundary, which needs machinery. And every product now has an address problem: made in one place, needed in another.

So the question this lesson answers is the one a sceptical engineer would ask.

Why would a cell pay for internal membranes at all?

The answer has three parts, and they are not obvious until you see them working. A compartment lets the cell run chemistries at the same time that would ruin each other in one shared volume. It lets the cell hold a local concentration far away from the concentration outside it. And because compartments sit in a fixed order along a route, passing through them imposes a fixed order on what gets done to a molecule.

Against those three purchases there is a standing bill, and the last scene of the lesson adds it up.

One sentence about emergence, then onwards

Cell theory, scale, and emergence (PREM-BIO-001) defined an emergent property as one belonging to an organisation of components and not to any component alone, and gave you a two-part test for it. Compartmentalisation is that same idea one level down: the cell is the organisation, the compartments are the components, and an acid interior or a proton gradient is a property of the arrangement and of nothing in it. Apply the test where it helps and do not make a mystery of it.

What you already need, and where to get it

Check
id check-prerequisite-architecture

Before reading on, answer from memory. The prerequisite topic on prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells compared two architectures. Which of the two has an interior divided by membranes into separate compartments, and which does most of its chemistry in one shared volume?

Then a harder one. If both kinds of cell run the same basic chemistry, what does that tell you about whether compartments are necessary for life?

Eukaryotic cells are the compartmentalised ones. Bacteria and archaea run most of their chemistry in a single internal volume, bounded by the plasma membrane and whatever surrounds it.

The second question is the one worth sitting with. Bacteria are alive, they are numerous, and they manage without an endomembrane system, so compartments are plainly not a requirement for being a cell. That reframes the whole question. Compartments are an investment a eukaryotic cell makes, and an investment is only sensible if it buys something. Everything below is an answer to what.

Recovery route

If the eukaryote-and-prokaryote comparison did not come back cleanly, that is the prerequisite topic for this lesson and not a gap you should paper over. Go back to Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells in the Cell Biology module and return here. What you need from it is small and specific: that a eukaryotic cell has a nucleus and an internal membrane system, that a bacterium generally does not, and that both are alive.

If the arithmetic in the next scene is the part that worries you, the tool it uses is a base-ten logarithm and nothing more. Logarithms and change (PREM-QNT-006) has the whole of it, and you can read the worked example there and come straight back.

What this lesson leaves alone

Two neighbouring questions are deliberately not answered here. What a membrane is actually made of, and why its behaviour changes with its composition, belongs to the lesson on membrane structure. How a specific molecule is moved across a membrane, against a gradient or down one, belongs to the lesson on membrane transport after it. This lesson treats a membrane as a boundary that can hold a difference, and asks what a cell does with that.

scenes.title: Do the arithmetic before you accept the number
scenes.contentHtml:
Do the arithmetic before you accept the number

Somewhere in the colonocyte you have just met there is a small sac called a lysosome, and the fluid inside it is acid. Not slightly acid. The cytosol around it sits near pH 7.2, and the lysosome runs somewhere around pH 5 and can be lower.

Written as pH values those two numbers look close together, which is exactly the trap. pH is a logarithmic scale, so a gap of two and a bit is not a small difference in a shared quantity. Work out how large it really is before reading on.

Check
id check-proton-ratio

Take the cytosol at pH 7.2 and the lysosome at pH 4.5, which is the acid end of the reported range.

  1. Write the hydrogen-ion concentration in each compartment as a power of ten.
  2. Divide one by the other. How many times more concentrated are hydrogen ions inside the lysosome than outside it?
  3. Say in one sentence what has to be true of the lysosomal membrane for that answer to be possible.

Attempt all three before you read the next paragraph. The third one is the point of the scene.

Working it through

The task. Two compartments, two stated pH values, and one question: what is the ratio of hydrogen-ion concentrations between them?

What is given, and what the symbols mean. pH is defined so that pH=−log10⁡[H+]\mathrm{pH} = -\log_{10}[\mathrm{H}^+], with the concentration in moles per litre. Rearranged, [H+]=10−pH[\mathrm{H}^+] = 10^{-\mathrm{pH}}. The two given values are cytosol 7.2 and lysosome 4.5, both dimensionless, both approximate.

Choosing the relation. The question asks for a ratio of concentrations, and the given quantities are logarithms of those concentrations. A ratio of two numbers is a difference of their logarithms, so the whole job is a subtraction followed by one power of ten. This is the reason the pH scale is worth having: it turns a factor into a gap you can read off by eye.

Execution. 102.710^{2.7} is a little over 500. In words: the lysosome holds hydrogen ions about five hundred times more concentrated than the fluid immediately outside it, across a boundary a few nanometres thick.

Check the arithmetic against the figure the literature quotes. Published work on lysosomes reports the hydrogen-ion gradient across the lysosomal membrane as 500 to 1000-fold, established and maintained by vacuolar-type proton pumps, the V-ATPases, which drive protons inward at the expense of ATP.

Be careful about what that comparison is worth. A quoted fold-difference of this kind is itself derived from pH values, so it is not an independent measurement of the gradient made by some other route. Our 500 and their 500 to 1000 are the same calculation done from similar inputs, and agreement between them confirms that the arithmetic is right, not that the pH values are. This is a consistency check on the working, and calling it anything stronger would be borrowing authority the comparison does not carry.

It is still worth doing. Had the arithmetic produced 5, or 50 000, something would have been wrong with an input or with the exponent, and that is exactly the class of error a check like this catches.

Interpretation. The answer to the third part of the check is now forced. A five-hundred-fold difference does not sit still on its own. Protons leak back down a gradient that steep, so something has to keep pushing them in, continuously, for as long as the lysosome exists. That something is a pump, and it runs on ATP.

What a compartment actually is

Definition
id definition-compartmentlabel Compartment

A compartment is a space inside a cell enclosed by membrane, holding conditions that differ from the cytosol and that are actively maintained against the tendency of those differences to even out. An organelle is a compartment, or in a few cases a structure, with a recognisable identity and a distinct job.

The operative word is maintained. A compartment is not a container that happens to hold something; it is a difference that costs energy to hold. Stop paying and the difference goes, while the membrane is still perfectly intact.

It is tempting to call a compartment a room, and the picture is useful for about one sentence. Rooms and compartments both let you keep incompatible things apart, and both need a way in and out. The mapping fails at the wall. A room's wall is passive: it does nothing, costs nothing to keep standing, and holds a temperature difference only until the heat leaks away. A compartment's boundary is loaded with pumps and channels, it is where a good deal of the chemistry actually happens, and holding the difference is a continuous expense. Once you have that, drop the room and use the real word.

The cell keeps several conditions at once

The lysosome is not one exception in an otherwise uniform interior. Measured across a mammalian cell, the pH landscape looks like this.

Compartment Approximate pH
Cytosol, nucleus, endoplasmic reticulum 7.2
Golgi network, falling from its entry face to its exit face 6.7 down to 6.0
Early and recycling endosomes 6.3 to 6.5
Late endosomes 5.5
Secretory granules 5.2 to 5.7
Lysosome, the most acidic 4.7 to 5.5 by one report, 4.5 to 5.0 by another

Read that table as a list of simultaneous conditions instead of a list of numbers. At this moment the same cell is holding a near-neutral compartment, a mildly acid one, and a strongly acid one, side by side, each one steady, each one costing energy. That is the first of the three purchases: incompatible chemistries running at the same time. A reaction that needs pH 5 and a reaction that needs pH 7.2 cannot both proceed in one shared volume, and a cell with one internal volume has to choose. A compartmentalised cell does not.

Notice also what the two reports of lysosomal pH do. They overlap and they disagree at the edges, because these are measurements on living cells using different probes and different cell types, not constants. Take about pH 5 as the working figure, remember it is a band, and do not carry a decimal place through a calculation that its inputs cannot support.

scenes.title: The membrane was never the whole of the protection
scenes.contentHtml:
The membrane was never the whole of the protection

Commit to an answer before reading on, because the answer you already hold is the thing worth examining.

Check
id check-burst-lysosome-prediction

A colonocyte contains lysosomes, each full of enzymes that break down the large molecules a cell is made of. Suppose one of them ruptured and emptied its entire contents into the cytosol.

Write down, in one sentence, what you expect to happen to that cell. Then write down what feature of the lysosome you think was preventing it.

The model most people arrive with

Stated fairly, it goes like this. A lysosome is a bag of digestive enzymes. Those enzymes would destroy the cell if they were loose in it, so the cell keeps them behind a membrane. The membrane is the safety device. Break the membrane and the cell digests itself.

Nothing in that is stupid, and part of it is true. Lysosomes really do contain enzymes that dismantle almost everything a cell is made of. They are where material taken in from outside ends up, and electron micrographs of normal cells show lysosomes with whole mitochondria inside them, being taken apart. The organelle really is where degradation happens.

The trouble is the second half: that the membrane is what stands between the cell and destruction.

The observation the model cannot survive

Every one of those enzymes is an acid hydrolase. That is not a description of where they live; it is a description of what they require. They achieve their activity in an acid environment, with optima around pH 4.5 to 5.0, which is why the organelle is held there at all.

Now put an acid hydrolase into cytosol at pH 7.2. It is more than two pH units above the conditions it needs, and it does very little. A cell-biology account of this puts it as double protection: the membrane normally keeps the digestive enzymes out of the cytosol, and even if they leaked out, they could do little damage at the cytosolic pH of about 7.2.

Read that carefully and the causal arrow reverses. The acid is half the containment, and not merely a service the cell provides so that its enzymes can work in comfort. It is what makes those enzymes safe to own.

The model that fits

Misconception
id misconception-membrane-as-walllabel The membrane is the safety device

The model to discard. A lysosome is a bag; its membrane is a wall; the wall is what protects the cell; breaching the wall releases active enzymes into the cytosol.

What it cannot explain. Why the enzymes require an acid environment at all, and why an organelle would spend ATP continuously to hold a five-hundred-fold proton gradient when a wall would already have done the job. On the wall model, the pH inside the lysosome is an incidental detail. It is not.

The model that replaces it. A compartment is a maintained condition, and the chemistry it holds runs properly only inside that condition. The lysosomal membrane and the pump in it produce an acid interior, and that acidity is a major part of why the hydrolases work there and do little elsewhere.

It is not the whole story, and the lesson should not pretend otherwise. Many of these enzymes are made as inactive precursors and are cleaved on the way, some need particular cofactors, and the acid interior also drives the processing that produces the mature form. So containment and activation are tightly coupled rather than the same act, and the honest claim is that a compartment supplies several of the conditions activity depends on at once, of which pH is the one this scene can demonstrate arithmetically.

Test the two models on one case. Consider a lysosome whose membrane is intact and whose enzyme content is completely normal, but whose interior has been allowed to drift up towards pH 7. The wall model predicts nothing much: the wall is standing, the enzymes are inside, digestion should carry on. The condition model predicts that digestion inside that lysosome slows or stops, because the enzymes are no longer near their optimum, and it predicts this even though nothing has leaked and nothing is missing. The two models disagree sharply, and that is what makes this a test rather than a restatement.

A second case where the chemistry has to be kept close

The lysosome is one way of segregating chemistry. The peroxisome is another, and it makes the general point from the opposite direction: instead of holding a condition, it holds a reaction and its clean-up in the same small volume.

Peroxisomes break down fatty acids that are too long for the mitochondria to start on, in a chain of oxidation steps. Those steps, and other peroxisomal oxidases, generate hydrogen peroxide as a by-product. Hydrogen peroxide is a reactive molecule and a cell would rather not have it wandering about. The peroxisome's answer is to carry catalase, an enzyme that decomposes hydrogen peroxide, in the same compartment where the peroxide is being produced.

That arrangement is worth pausing on, and worth stating carefully. Nothing here is locked away absolutely. Hydrogen peroxide can cross membranes, and cells use it deliberately as a signal elsewhere, so the peroxisome is not a sealed box. What colocalising the oxidases with catalase buys is that the peroxide is destroyed close to where it is made, which limits how much accumulates and how far the rest of the cell is exposed. Segregation here is a matter of degree, and the useful lesson is that keeping a reaction and its remedy together is often cheaper than keeping a product away from everything.

Both organelles are answering the same design problem in different ways: chemistry the cell needs, and chemistry the cell cannot afford to have everywhere. That is what the first purchase actually buys.

Recheck, in a case you have not seen

Check
id check-recheck-conditions

A cell contains a compartment holding an enzyme that works best at pH 5. The enzyme is made in the endoplasmic reticulum, which sits at about pH 7.2, and travels through the Golgi, which runs from about 6.7 down to about 6.0, before arriving.

  1. During that journey the enzyme passes through the cell carrying its full digestive capacity. Why is the cargo it travels alongside not destroyed on the way?
  2. Which of the two models from this scene does your answer use?
  3. Name one thing your answer assumes that the numbers alone do not establish.

The route runs from a near-neutral compartment through a mildly acid one, and only the destination is strongly acid. An enzyme with an optimum near pH 5 is below its best performance for the whole journey and reaches full activity only on arrival. The condition model gives that answer directly; the wall model has nothing to say about it, because on the wall model the enzyme is equally dangerous everywhere and its safety is purely a matter of which side of a membrane it is on.

The assumption worth naming is that each enzyme's activity falls away smoothly and substantially as pH rises above its optimum, and by enough to matter over a difference of one to two pH units. Optima differ between enzymes, and how steeply activity falls either side of an optimum is a property of the particular enzyme. The two published figures used here establish where the compartments sit and that the lysosomal environment is optimal for these enzymes. The inference that a hydrolase is substantially less effective at Golgi pH follows from that, and it is an inference, so it is labelled as one.

scenes.title: An acid compartment is no use if the enzyme never arrives
scenes.contentHtml:
An acid compartment is no use if the enzyme never arrives

Dividing a cell into compartments creates a problem the undivided cell did not have. Every protein is built by a ribosome, and ribosomes start work in the cytosol. The hydrolase that has to end up at pH 5, the pump that has to end up on the apical face and nowhere else, the enzyme that has to end up inside a peroxisome: all of them begin in the same place, and none of them belongs there.

So a compartmentalised cell needs a postal system. Each newly made protein has to find its way from a ribosome to its working location by a specific route, guided by signals in its own amino-acid sequence. That is a real, separate piece of machinery, and it is a large part of what compartmentalisation costs.

The route, once

Take that route one step at a time, because each step is answering a different question.

Where the instructions are kept. The nucleus holds the main genome and is the principal site of DNA and RNA synthesis. Translation happens outside it, on ribosomes in the cytosol. That separation of where a message is written from where it is read is itself a compartment doing work, and later lessons in this course use it heavily.

How a protein gets diverted off the default path. Translation starts in the cytosol for every nucleus-encoded protein, which is nearly all of them; the thirteen proteins encoded by mitochondrial DNA are translated by mitochondrial ribosomes inside the mitochondrion and never join this route. For everything on the route taught here, about thirty per cent of newly synthesised ones are pulled off that default course almost immediately. As the first stretch of the new chain emerges from the ribosome, a signal sequence in it is recognised and captured by a particle called the signal recognition particle, which carries the whole ribosome-and-chain assembly to the endoplasmic reticulum membrane and hands the signal sequence over to a channel there, the Sec61 translocon. The chain is then threaded across the membrane as it is made.

Notice what kind of thing that is. The address is part of the product, readable while the product is still being built, and it is read by a receptor whose job is to recognise it. No sorting office attaches it afterwards. Compartmentalisation obliges a cell to encode a destination in every item it makes.

What the sequence of compartments does to the product. Once inside the endoplasmic reticulum the protein folds. From there it moves on through the Golgi apparatus, and along that path it passes through a series of compartments where it is successively modified. Order matters here: the same protein arriving at the Golgi is not the object that left the ribosome, and it will not be the object that leaves the Golgi.

This is the second purchase. A fixed order of compartments imposes a fixed order of operations. A cell with one internal volume would have to control the sequence of a dozen modifications some other way, with every enzyme present in the same solution at the same time. A cell with a route gets the sequence for free from the geometry.

How the cell decides where it goes next. The route ends at the trans-Golgi network, which is where sorting happens. It packages finished proteins into transport vesicles and dispatches them to their specific destinations. The clearest worked case is the lysosome: enzymes bound for lysosomes have mannose 6-phosphate groups added to their sugar chains as they pass through the Golgi, those groups are recognised by mannose 6-phosphate receptors in the trans-Golgi network, and the tagged enzyme is diverted accordingly.

A chemical tag, and a receptor that reads it. That is the whole address system in miniature, and it explains something the previous scene left open: how the hydrolases and the acid compartment ever find each other, given that they are made in different places by different machinery.

The extra axis a polarised cell has to sort on

For a cell that is not polarised, the plasma membrane is one destination. For the colonocyte it is two. The apical face and the basolateral face carry different proteins and do different work, so a vesicle leaving the trans-Golgi network cannot simply be addressed to "the surface". It has to be addressed to a face.

Hold on to that, because it is where the lesson ends. A cell that has to sort to two surfaces has a delivery step that can fail on its own, without anything being wrong with manufacture. The final scene is a case where exactly that happens.

Retrieval, before you move on

Check
id check-route-failure-points

A colonocyte makes a transport protein whose working location is the apical membrane.

  1. Name the step at which this protein first leaves the default cytosolic route, and say what physically causes it to leave.
  2. Two different faults are possible: the protein could be built wrongly, or it could be built correctly and delivered wrongly. For each, say where in the route you would look.
  3. If a fault removed the mannose 6-phosphate tag from a lysosomal enzyme, where would you predict that enzyme ends up, and why?

The protein leaves the cytosolic route at the ribosome, as soon as its signal sequence emerges and is caught by the signal recognition particle. A fault of manufacture shows up early, in the sequence itself or in folding inside the endoplasmic reticulum, and the product is defective wherever it goes. A fault of delivery shows up after the trans-Golgi network, and the product is intact but in the wrong place. Those are different diagnoses with different consequences, and separating them is the skill this lesson is training.

For the third: an untagged lysosomal enzyme has nothing for the mannose 6-phosphate receptors to recognise, so it is not diverted at the sorting step. It stays in the default flow of the secretory route, which runs to the cell surface, and leaves the cell. The lysosome is not damaged and the enzyme is not defective. It is simply not there. Predicting that from the tag alone is the point of understanding the address system as a separate system.

scenes.title: Where the compartment is the machine
scenes.contentHtml:
Where the compartment is the machine

Everything so far treats a compartment as a place with conditions: somewhere to put chemistry, or somewhere to put it in order. The mitochondrion is different, and the difference is worth a scene of its own, because getting it wrong is what makes "the powerhouse of the cell" such a useless thing to have memorised.

Here is the mechanism in one pass. Oxidising fuel releases energy, and a mitochondrion does not use that energy directly to make ATP. It uses it to pump protons across a membrane, building an electrical and chemical potential difference between the two sides. Then it lets the protons flow back, and the returning flow turns the rotor of an enzyme, ATP synthase, which makes ATP as it turns. The energy takes a detour through a gradient before it becomes chemistry.

Now ask what that arrangement requires. A gradient is a difference between two sides. It does not exist in a substance; it exists across a boundary. There is no such thing as a proton gradient in an open volume, in the same way there is no such thing as a pressure difference in a room with no wall down the middle.

So the membrane here belongs to the mechanism. Oxidative phosphorylation requires a membrane to couple the transport of protons to the synthesis of ATP; take the membrane away and you have not removed a wrapper, you have removed the machine. Chemical uncouplers make the same point experimentally: they let protons cross the membrane freely, which dissipates the proton potential, and respiration then proceeds while ATP synthesis falls to nothing. Fuel is still being burnt. Nothing is stored, because there is nowhere for the difference to sit.

That is why the label is unhelpful. A power station is a building containing generators, and you could in principle move the generators outdoors. You cannot move this one outdoors. Say instead that a mitochondrion is a compartment whose boundary holds a gradient, and the mechanism follows from the sentence.

What this particular cell is burning

Ask what a mature colonocyte is actually burning, and the crypt argument closes on itself. Seventy to eighty per cent of its energy comes from butyrate, a short-chain fatty acid, oxidised to carbon dioxide by the mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation system. That is the machinery just described, running at high load.

Where does the butyrate come from? It is made by the bacteria in the lumen, on the other side of the apical membrane, as a product of their fermentation. The cell described at the start of this lesson takes up a fuel manufactured by the population it is keeping out of the tissue.

That metabolism has a measurable consequence. Mature colonocytes running this way consume oxygen heavily, which holds the oxygen partial pressure at the epithelium below 7.6 mmHg, under one per cent oxygen. The surface of the colonic lining is a hypoxic place, and it is hypoxic because of what is happening inside the mitochondria of the cells that make it up.

Stop there instead of going one step further. Whether that epithelial hypoxia is what maintains the anaerobic community in the lumen is an active research question and a claim this lesson does not make. What is established is the direction of the arrow so far: bacterial fermentation supplies the fuel, mitochondrial compartments burn it, and the oxygen tension at the tissue surface is a consequence.

Note also what kind of property that is. No single mitochondrion has an oxygen tension. Epithelial hypoxia belongs to a sheet of cells all consuming oxygen at once, which is the emergence test from the first lesson applied at tissue scale to a process that starts inside an organelle.

Adding up the bill

The purchases are on the table. Here is the invoice.

Building material. Every compartment needs a boundary, and boundaries are built from lipid and protein that the cell has to synthesise. Membrane-enclosed compartments take up close to half a cell's volume, so this is not a marginal expense.

Standing energy. Each maintained condition leaks. The V-ATPase pumps protons into the lysosome for as long as the lysosome exists, using ATP to do it, because a five-hundred-fold gradient runs down the moment you stop. That cost never ends and it never falls.

Crossing charges. In an undivided cell a molecule made in one place is already everywhere it needs to be. Once you have boundaries, everything that has to get from one side to the other needs a transporter, a channel, or a vesicle, and each of those is a protein the cell has to make, place and regulate.

Addressing. Every product needs a destination encoded in it and a receptor able to read the code: signal sequences read by the signal recognition particle, mannose 6-phosphate read by mannose 6-phosphate receptors, and a separate apparatus again for sorting to the apical face against the basolateral face.

Set that against what it buys. Incompatible chemistries at once, which is how a cell can hold a compartment at pH 5 and another near 7.2 and let both work. Local concentration, which is how hydrogen ions can be five hundred times more concentrated in one small volume than a nanometre away. Controlled sequence, which is how a fixed order of compartments gives a fixed order of modifications without needing a controller. And a fourth thing this scene added: a boundary that is itself the working part of an energy-converting device.

What most bacteria lack is not membranes, energetics, or targeting. They build membranes, they run a proton-motive force across the plasma membrane and make ATP from it, they localise proteins to particular places, and some carry genuine internal compartments: the carboxysome is one, and the two-centimetre bacterium from the previous lesson has membrane-bound chromosome compartments. What they mostly lack is the eukaryotic endomembrane system, the set of internal compartments with a sorting route between them that this scene has been describing.

So the investment is real and its scale is optional, and the rest of this module is about what a cell does with the expensive version.

Check
id check-uncoupler-versus-pump-block

Two hypothetical interventions on the same colonocyte, each affecting one compartment.

  1. An agent makes the mitochondrial inner membrane freely permeable to protons.
  2. An agent stops the V-ATPase in the lysosomal membrane.

For each, say which of the three purchases is being attacked, and predict what stops working. Then say what the two cases have in common that a list of organelle names would not have told you.

The first attacks the gradient itself. Protons stop accumulating on one side, the potential difference collapses, and ATP synthesis stops even though fuel is still being oxidised and every protein in the mitochondrion is intact. The second attacks a maintained condition. Protons stop being driven into the lysosome, the interior drifts towards the cytosolic pH, the acid hydrolases move away from their optimum, and digestion inside an undamaged lysosome full of undamaged enzymes slows.

What the two have in common is the shape of the failure. In neither case is a component broken. In both cases a difference has been lost, and everything that depended on the difference stops. That is what it means to say a compartment is a maintained condition rather than a container, and it is not a fact you can reach by learning which organelle is which.

scenes.title: Name the condition, then predict the failure
scenes.contentHtml:
Name the condition, then predict the failure

Everything in this lesson reduces to one habit. Given a job a cell has to do, do not ask which organelle does it. Ask what condition the job needs, and then ask which compartment holds that condition. The organelle name is the last thing you work out, not the first.

Three passes below, with less help each time. Work each one before reading the response under it.

Pass one, with the reasoning laid out

A colonocyte takes in a fragment of bacterial protein from the lumen and needs it broken down to amino acids it can reuse.

Worked in full, so the shape is visible:

  • The job. Cutting peptide bonds, thoroughly, on material of unpredictable composition.
  • The condition it needs. The enzymes that do this work are acid hydrolases, at their optimum around pH 4.5 to 5.0. So the job needs a small volume held at that pH, separated from a cytosol at 7.2 where those enzymes would achieve very little.
  • The compartment that holds it. The lysosome, which the cell maintains near pH 5 by pumping protons inward with a V-ATPase.
  • Remove the condition and what fails. Stop the pump and the interior drifts up towards 7.2. The membrane is intact, the enzymes are all present, and the digestion stops anyway. That last sentence is the one to carry forward.

Pass two, with the first step given

An oxidation reaction the cell needs to run on a very-long-chain fatty acid produces hydrogen peroxide as a by-product. Hydrogen peroxide is reactive and the cell would rather it did not circulate.

The condition here is not a pH. It is proximity: the requirement is that the peroxide is destroyed close enough to where it is made that it never travels.

You finish it. Which compartment holds that condition, what does it contain that meets the requirement, and how is this a different solution from the lysosome's?

Check
id check-practice-peroxisome

Answer the three parts above in writing before reading on. The third part is the one that matters.

The peroxisome. It carries catalase, which decomposes hydrogen peroxide, in the same compartment as the oxidases producing it, so production and disposal are a few tens of nanometres apart. The solution differs from the lysosome's in what is being segregated. A lysosome segregates a capability: the enzymes are kept where their conditions are, and are largely harmless outside. A peroxisome segregates a transient product: the peroxide is never meant to leave, and the compartment exists so that a reactive intermediate can be at a working concentration in one small volume and nowhere else.

Pass three, on your own

Check
id check-practice-independent

Three situations. For each, name the condition the job requires, name the compartment or route involved, and say what you would predict if the named element failed. One of the three has no compartment in the answer, and identifying which is part of the task.

  1. A pump protein has to end up in the apical membrane of a colonocyte and nowhere else. The gene is normal, the protein folds normally, and the trans-Golgi network packages it. Vesicle delivery to the apical face fails.
  2. An enzyme has to reach the lysosome. Every step of manufacture is normal, but the mannose 6-phosphate tag is never added in the Golgi.
  3. An enzyme does its work in the cytosol at pH 7.2 and is needed nowhere else.

Then, across all three: which are failures of manufacture and which are failures of delivery?

One. The condition is a location: this protein works only on the face that meets the lumen, so the requirement is delivery to a specific face rather than to "the surface". Break vesicle delivery to that face and the protein exists, folded and functional, sitting in the wrong place. Predict a cell that is alive, that is making everything it should, and that cannot do the apical job. Hold this one; the last scene is a real version of it.

Two. The condition is an address that a receptor can read. With no mannose 6-phosphate group there is nothing for the mannose 6-phosphate receptors to recognise at the sorting step, so the enzyme is not diverted, stays in the default outward flow of the secretory route, and leaves the cell. The lysosome is undamaged and the enzyme is not defective. It is simply somewhere else, and the digestive capacity of the lysosome falls because of an addressing failure rather than a manufacturing one.

Three. This is the one without a compartment. About thirty per cent of newly made proteins are diverted into the endoplasmic reticulum route; being diverted is the special case, and a protein with no signal sequence stays in the cytosol because nothing removes it. The right answer is that no compartment is needed and none is used. A learner who has started sorting everything into organelles will invent one here, and inventing one is the error the item is looking for.

Across the three: the first two are delivery failures, and neither involves a defective product. The third has no failure in it. Nothing here is a failure of manufacture, which is deliberate, because the manufacture story is the one most learners already have and the delivery story is the one this lesson is adding.

Where to go if a pass went wrong

Each failure has a specific route back, and none of them is "read the lesson again".

If pass one went wrong at the condition rather than at the name, reread the second scene, and particularly the arithmetic. The number five hundred is what makes the difference between a container and a maintained condition concrete.

If pass two produced an answer about the peroxisome keeping something locked away from the cell, reread the second half of the third scene. The distinction between segregating a capability and segregating a transient product is the whole of that pass.

If pass three's third item produced an organelle, that is the most useful mistake in the lesson and it means the framing has overshot. Return to the last part of the first scene: bacteria run almost everything in one volume, so a compartment is never the default answer to anything.

If the two kinds of failure ran together, work the diagram in the fourth scene backwards from each destination and say at which step each fault would first become visible.

Accessibility and alternatives

Nothing in this lesson requires seeing a picture. The route diagram in the fourth scene carries a long description that states every node, every step, the pH of each compartment, and the three destinations, in the order the argument uses them, and the surrounding prose walks the same route in sentences. The pH landscape in the second scene is a table of text, and the two quantities that matter, cytosol 7.2 and lysosome about 5, appear in the prose as well as in the table.

All arithmetic is written out in words and symbols together: the ratio is a subtraction of two pH values followed by one power of ten, and the equation and its plain reading sit next to each other. No prompt, answer, or piece of feedback depends on colour, position, animation, hover, or timing, and no task asks you to drag anything. Every check can be answered in writing and reread as often as you like.

scenes.title: Clinical wrap-up: everything was built, and none of it arrived
scenes.contentHtml:
Clinical wrap-up: everything was built, and none of it arrived

Callout
id callout-teaching-boundary

Teaching example, not medical advice. The infant below is invented. The condition described is real and the findings quoted come from published review, but nothing here is a diagnostic criterion, a threshold, a test performance, a management plan, or a statement of what any finding would mean in any real patient. This is a reasoning exercise about compartments and delivery.

An invented newborn, a few days old, has watery diarrhoea that does not stop and does not respond to withholding feeds. The infant is losing weight and losing water faster than it can be replaced by mouth. A small-bowel biopsy is taken.

Under the microscope the epithelium is there. The cells are present, they are alive, they are the right shape and in the right place. What is missing is the brush border: the apical surface has few microvilli, or abnormal ones, or none. Staining for a protein that belongs on the apical membrane does not find it on the surface. It finds it in a band just underneath, inside the cell. There are vesicle-like structures in the cytoplasm, and in some cells there are microvilli sitting inside an intracellular inclusion, pointing into a space that has no business existing.

This is microvillus inclusion disease, and everything you need to reason about it is in the fourth scene of this lesson.

First, note where we have gone

This case leaves the colon. Microvillus inclusion disease presents as a severe neonatal enteropathy and its biopsy findings are described in small-bowel tissue, where the same absorptive architecture appears on villi instead of around crypts. The absorptive cell, its apical brush border and its basolateral face are the ones you have been working with all lesson. Take the case, then come back: the colonocyte is the running example for the rest of this module.

Work it with the lesson's own tools

Which face does the job, and what is on it? The absorptive cell's uptake happens across the apical surface, and the microvilli of the brush border are what make that surface large enough to be worth using. Around a thousand of them on a mature cell, packed together. The basolateral face, doing a different job, is not affected in the way the apical one is.

Is this a failure of manufacture or of delivery? Pass three of the practice scene asked exactly this question, and the answer here is delivery. The disease is caused by mutations in genes for myosin Vb, syntaxin 3 or syntaxin binding protein 2. Those are not genes for brush-border proteins. They are genes for the machinery that moves vesicles and fuses them with the plasma membrane, so what fails is vesicle trafficking or vesicle fusion, and the consequence reported is that vesicles carrying apical proteins accumulate subapically.

Read that against the diagram. Manufacture is intact: transcription, translation, entry into the endoplasmic reticulum, folding, modification through the Golgi, sorting in the trans-Golgi network. The cargo is made, addressed and packaged. The last leg fails, and the cargo stops one step short of where it belongs.

Does the model predict what the pathologist sees? It predicts three things, and all three are what is reported. Apical proteins should be found subapically instead of on the surface, and they are. The brush border should be absent or abnormal, because it is built from material that has to be delivered to that face, and it is. Vesicles that cannot fuse where they were meant to should be visible as accumulated intracellular structures, and they are, along with the inclusions the disease is named for.

Does the model predict the clinical picture? Partly, and the gap is instructive. Extremely watery diarrhoea from the first days of life, with dehydration and weight loss, is what published description reports.

A missing absorptive surface is part of that, but the review this case rests on says plainly that reduced surface area does not fully account for the fluid loss. The trafficking defect does not disable the cell evenly: transporters that have to reach the apical surface are the ones that fail to arrive, while secretory routes are less affected, so the balance between absorption and secretion is disturbed as well as the surface being smaller. How much each contributes varies between genotypes and between model systems.

That is the more useful lesson for a scene about compartments and delivery. A sorting failure is not a uniform loss of function; it removes whatever depended on the route that broke, and what depended on other routes carries on.

Why this belongs in a lesson about organelles

Nothing has gone wrong with any organelle's condition. The lysosomes are still acid. The mitochondria still hold their gradient. The endoplasmic reticulum still folds proteins and the Golgi still modifies them. Every compartment in this lesson is working.

What has failed is the fourth item on the bill: the system that gets each product to the compartment or the face where it works. The first scene said that internal membranes create an address problem that an undivided cell does not have, and that solving it is part of the price. A disease of the delivery machinery is what that line item looks like when it is not paid.

That is also why "organelle" is a poor unit of understanding on its own. A list of organelles and their functions has no place to put this case. A cell described as a set of maintained conditions connected by routes has exactly one place to put it, and it is the arrow between two boxes.

The thread back to the crypt

The absorptive cell in a colonic crypt lives about four to five days, and the whole lining is rebuilt continuously. Every one of those cells has to construct its own brush border, its own apical and basolateral protein sets, and its own complement of compartments, from scratch, within a few days of being born at the crypt base. The delivery machinery in this lesson is not doing a job once. It is doing it in every cell of a tissue that never stops replacing itself.

The next lessons take the parts of that apart. What a membrane is made of, and why the apical membrane of this cell is built differently from its basolateral membrane, is the lesson on membrane structure. How sodium and glucose actually cross it, and why that matters for treating the dehydration in the case above, is the lesson on membrane transport after it. Both are questions this lesson deliberately left standing.

What you should be able to do now

Three things, and each has an assessment item.

Given a stated cellular job, name the condition it requires and the compartment that maintains it, and justify the pairing by the condition rather than by the organelle's name. Compute a concentration ratio between two compartments from their pH values, check it against an independently reported figure, and say what holding that difference costs. Predict where a product ends up, and what stops working, when a named step of the route from gene to working location fails, separating a fault of manufacture from a fault of delivery.

The mastery check holds four untimed, retakeable items worth twelve points. Attempt each before opening its reasoning. A missed criterion routes you to a different case, never the same one twice.

items.prompt: Three jobs a cell has to do. First, run an oxidation whose by-product is a reactive molecule that must not circulate. Second, use an enzyme that achieves its activity only in strongly acid conditions. Third, make ATP by letting protons flow down a difference in their concentration. For each job, name the condition the job requires before you name any organelle, then name the compartment that maintains that condition. Then, for each, state what would stop working if that condition alone were lost while every protein involved remained present and intact. One of the three is different in kind from the other two; say which and why.

answer.correct: The first job requires that the reactive product be destroyed where it is made, so that its journey is short. That condition is met in the peroxisome, which holds catalase in the same compartment as the oxidases producing hydrogen peroxide. Remove the condition, by having catalase somewhere else, and hydrogen peroxide leaves the compartment before it is decomposed even though every enzyme is present and working. The second job requires an acid environment, around pH 4.5 to 5.0, held against a cytosol near 7.2. That condition is maintained in the lysosome by a proton pump that consumes ATP. Stop the pump and the interior drifts towards 7.2, the acid hydrolases fall away from their optimum, and digestion inside an undamaged lysosome full of undamaged enzymes slows. The third job requires a difference in proton concentration between two sides of a boundary. That is the mitochondrion, where the electron transport chain pumps protons across the membrane and their return flow drives ATP synthase. Make the boundary freely permeable to protons and the potential collapses, so respiration continues while ATP synthesis stops. The third is different in kind. In the first two, the compartment holds a condition in which chemistry happens; in the third, the compartment boundary is part of the mechanism, because a gradient is a difference between two sides and cannot exist without a boundary. Removing the boundary there does not open the device, it removes it.
answer.summary: Proximity of production and disposal in the peroxisome; an acid interior held by a pump in the lysosome; a proton difference across a boundary in the mitochondrion, which is the one where the compartment is the mechanism rather than the setting.
answer.reasoning: Award one point when all three conditions are stated before the organelle names and each condition is the right one: co-localisation of production and disposal, an acid environment maintained against the cytosol, and a proton-concentration difference across a boundary. A response that leads with organelle names and then justifies them does not earn this point, because naming first is the habit the item exists to test. Award one point for three failure predictions in which the components stay intact and the function stops anyway. Award one point for identifying the mitochondrion as different in kind and giving the reason, that a gradient exists only across a boundary, so the boundary is the mechanism and not the setting. On a retry, run the same three steps for a compartment that must keep newly made proteins away from cytosolic conditions while they fold, and for a compartment that must modify a protein in a fixed order.
acceptableResponses: Any response that names proximity of production and disposal, a maintained acid environment, and a proton difference across a boundary as the three conditions, attaches each to the peroxisome, lysosome and mitochondrion respectively, predicts a functional failure in each case with the components intact, and singles out the mitochondrion on the ground that a gradient requires two sides.
commonErrors: Naming the organelle first and reverse-engineering a condition to fit it
Giving the peroxisome's condition as containment of a poison rather than destruction close to the site of production
Predicting that the enzymes are destroyed or lost when the condition is removed, rather than that they remain and stop being effective
Treating the mitochondrion as a container of ATP-making machinery, which loses the reason it is different in kind
Answering the third case with the citric acid cycle or the electron transport chain as the condition, which names a process instead of the difference the process maintains

items.prompt: The cytosol sits at pH 7.2. Take one compartment at pH 6.0 and a second at pH 4.5. Compute the ratio of hydrogen-ion concentrations between each compartment and the cytosol, showing the arithmetic. Then give the factor by which the second compartment's gradient exceeds the first, and obtain that factor twice: once by dividing your two answers and once directly from the two compartment pH values. Say what the comparison implies about the relative standing energy cost of the two compartments, and name one quantity this comparison cannot give you.

answer.correct:
Because pH is minus the base-ten logarithm of hydrogen-ion concentration, a ratio of concentrations is ten raised to the difference of the pH values. For the compartment at 6.0 the ratio is 10 to the power (7.2 minus 6.0), that is 10 to the power 1.2, about 16. For the compartment at 4.5 it is 10 to the power (7.2 minus 4.5), that is 10 to the power 2.7, a little over 500. Dividing, about 500 over about 16 is roughly thirty, so the more acidic compartment sits about thirty times further from the cytosol in hydrogen-ion concentration than the other one does.

What the arithmetic does not license is a claim about which compartment costs more to maintain. A concentration ratio gives the thermodynamic work per proton moved; the power a cell actually spends holding a compartment there also depends on how leaky its membrane is, how much membrane there is, the membrane potential, and how the pumps are regulated, none of which is given. Credit is for the two ratios, the comparison between them, and for saying that relative ATP use cannot be inferred from pH alone.
answer.summary: About 16-fold at pH 6.0 and about 500-fold at pH 4.5, the second steeper than the first by about 32, obtained either by division or directly from the 1.5 pH-unit gap; a steeper gradient implies a larger standing cost, but no pH value yields an ATP consumption rate.
answer.reasoning: Award one point for both ratios computed as ten raised to a pH difference, giving about 16 and about 500, with the reasoning shown rather than the answers asserted. Award one point for obtaining the factor of about 32 by both routes and saying why they must agree. Award one point for the interpretation: a steeper gradient leaks harder and costs more to hold, together with a named quantity the arithmetic cannot supply, such as the rate of ATP consumption or the leak rate, with a reason. On a retry, do the same for a compartment at pH 5.5 against a cytosol at 7.4, and compare it with a compartment at pH 6.8, then say what changes and what does not when the cytosolic reference moves. The common over-reach on this item is to conclude that the more acidic compartment leaks harder and therefore costs more. It may, but nothing in the stem establishes it.

Values within about twenty per cent are correct, since the inputs are approximate.
commonErrors: Subtracting the pH values and reporting the difference itself as the ratio, so 1.2 is given instead of about 16
Dividing the pH values instead of subtracting them
Getting the sign the wrong way round, so the more acid compartment comes out less concentrated in hydrogen ions
Reporting a ratio to several significant figures from inputs given to one decimal place
Concluding that the more acid compartment consumes a specific amount of ATP, which the pH values do not determine
Naming a quantity the comparison cannot give without saying why it is not contained in a pH value

items.prompt: In a colonocyte, a mutation removes the signal sequence from a protein whose working location is the apical membrane. The rest of the amino-acid sequence is unchanged and the protein is still translated normally. Which statement predicts the outcome, and for the right reason?

options.text: It is made on a cytosolic ribosome and stays in the cytosol, because nothing diverts it into the endoplasmic reticulum, so it never reaches the Golgi, is never sorted, and arrives at neither face.
It reaches the basolateral membrane instead, because a protein that loses its apical address defaults to the other face.
It reaches the apical membrane anyway, because the trans-Golgi network sorts cargo by destination and would recognise this protein.
It is delivered to the lysosome and degraded, because a protein with no address is disposed of.

answer.summary: It stays in the cytosol, because the signal sequence is what diverts a protein out of the default cytosolic route, and losing it means the protein never enters the route at all.
answer.reasoning: The signal sequence acts at the very first branch point, while the chain is still emerging from the ribosome. Removing it removes the diversion, so the protein is completed in the cytosol and no later step of the route ever sees it. The basolateral option treats the two surface addresses as a pair with a default, which they are not; sorting between them happens in the trans-Golgi network, and this protein never gets there. The trans-Golgi option puts the failure at the wrong step: sorting can only act on cargo that has arrived, and the point of this item is that arrival is what failed. The lysosome option invents a disposal rule the lesson does not teach and that the mannose 6-phosphate route contradicts, since reaching a lysosome is itself an addressed delivery and not a default. On a retry, predict the outcome when the signal sequence is intact but the mannose 6-phosphate transferase in the Golgi is missing, and say at which step the two cases diverge.
commonErrors: Assuming the two cell surfaces are alternatives with a default, so losing one address sends the protein to the other
Locating the failure at the sorting step instead of at entry to the route
Inventing an automatic disposal route for unaddressed proteins
Answering correctly that the protein stays in the cytosol but giving the number of proteins on the endoplasmic reticulum route as the reason rather than the diversion mechanism

items.prompt: An invented laboratory group works on cultured intestinal epithelial cells and plans two separate interventions. Predict what each would produce, working only from the mechanisms in this lesson. Intervention A blocks the addition of mannose 6-phosphate groups in the Golgi and changes nothing else. Intervention B blocks the proton pump in the lysosomal membrane and changes nothing else. (1) For each, say whether it attacks a maintained condition or the addressing system, and predict what happens to the cell's ability to break down material it has taken in. (2) In intervention A, predict where the soluble lysosomal enzymes end up, with your reason. (3) In intervention B the lysosomal interior is stated to drift from pH 4.6 to pH 6.4; compute the factor by which the hydrogen-ion concentration inside falls. (4) The group argues that intervention B is the safer of the two for the cell, because nothing is released from the lysosome. Judge that argument using this lesson's model of what protects the cytosol. (5) Name two things these predictions do not establish. Nothing in this item describes a real study, device, patient or clinical procedure, and none of it is guidance for any real investigation.

answer.correct: Intervention A attacks the addressing system. The soluble lysosomal enzymes are made and folded normally and travel the route normally, but with no mannose 6-phosphate group there is nothing for the mannose 6-phosphate receptors in the trans-Golgi network to recognise, so they are not diverted at the sorting step. They stay in the default outward flow of the secretory route and are predicted to leave the cell, appearing outside it rather than inside a lysosome. The lysosome is undamaged and the enzymes are not defective; the cell's capacity to break down material it has taken in falls because the enzymes are not there. Intervention B attacks a maintained condition. The pump stops, protons are no longer driven inward, and the interior drifts towards the cytosolic pH. The enzymes are all present and the membrane is intact, and degradation slows anyway because the hydrolases are no longer near their acid optimum. From pH 4.6 to pH 6.4 is a rise of 1.8 pH units, so the hydrogen-ion concentration falls by ten to the power 1.8, a factor of about 63. The group's safety argument misreads the model. On the picture in which the membrane is the whole protection, a rupture is the dangerous event and a pH drift is harmless. This lesson's model says the cytosol is doubly protected: a rupture releases hydrolases that can do little at the cytosolic pH of about 7.2, while the pH drift disables the digestion the cell actually needs, inside an organelle that is still intact. Neither intervention is safe, they fail differently, and the one the group calls safer is the one that removes the function. Two things these predictions do not establish, among others: what fraction of the untagged enzymes actually leaves the cell, since no source here reports that; and how much hydrolase activity survives at pH 6.4, since no activity-versus-pH curve for a named enzyme was supplied and the loss is inferred from the optimum rather than measured. A third is the specificity of intervention B, since the same family of proton pumps acidifies the Golgi, endosomes and secretory granules, so blocking it in the lysosome alone is an idealisation of the item rather than a property of a real reagent.
answer.summary: A is an addressing failure that sends undamaged enzymes out of the cell; B is a lost condition that stops digestion inside an intact organelle; the pH drift of 1.8 units is a fall of about 63-fold in hydrogen-ion concentration; the safety argument mistakes the loss of function for safety; and the predictions establish neither the fraction of enzyme lost nor the residual activity, and treat the pump block as compartment-specific when it is not.
answer.reasoning: Award one point for classifying A as an addressing failure and B as a lost maintained condition, with both predicted to reduce degradation by different routes and with the components intact in each case. Award one point for the destination in A, outside the cell by the default secretory flow, with the reason given as the absent tag and the unrecognising receptor rather than as damage. Award one point for the arithmetic: 1.8 pH units, ten to the power 1.8, about 63, computed rather than asserted. Award one point for judging the safety argument against the double-protection model and for naming two genuine limits of the prediction with reasons. On a retry, review a third intervention in which the vesicles carrying tagged enzymes are made normally and reach the lysosome but cannot fuse with it, and say which of the two failure types that is and what the cell would show.
acceptableResponses: Any response that separates the addressing failure from the lost condition, predicts secretion of the untagged enzymes with the receptor as the reason, computes about a 63-fold fall from a 1.8 pH-unit rise, rejects the safety argument by way of the double protection, and names two limits with reasons, such as the unknown fraction secreted, the unmeasured residual activity at pH 6.4, or the non-specificity of a proton-pump block.
commonErrors: Treating intervention A as a manufacturing fault, so the enzymes are described as defective rather than misdelivered
Predicting that untagged enzymes are destroyed, which invents a disposal route the lesson does not teach
Reporting the pH change of 1.8 units as the answer instead of raising ten to that power
Agreeing that intervention B is safer because nothing is released, which is the membrane-as-wall model reappearing
Concluding that a rupture would be harmless, which overshoots the double-protection statement in the other direction
Naming limits that are generic, such as this is only a model, instead of limits the sources and arithmetic actually leave open
Treating the lysosome-only pump block as achievable, when the same pump family acidifies several compartments

claims.scope: The requirement that makes the mitochondrial boundary part of the mechanism rather than a container around it.
claims.uncertainty: The statement concerns the requirement for a membrane, not the detailed topology of the mitochondrial inner membrane or the arrangement of its cristae, neither of which this lesson teaches.

claims.statement: The electron transport chain creates a proton potential gradient across the mitochondrial membrane during respiration, and the flow of protons back down that gradient turns the rotor of ATP synthase, which synthesises ATP as it turns.
claims.scope: The mechanism by which a compartment boundary stores energy as a difference and converts it to chemistry, at the level of detail a first lesson on compartmentalisation needs.
claims.uncertainty: The lesson does not teach the composition of the electron transport chain, the stoichiometry of proton pumping, or the structure of the synthase. Those belong to later lessons on metabolism.

claims.statement: Classical chemical uncouplers such as 2,4-dinitrophenol dissipate the proton potential across the mitochondrial membrane, so respiration proceeds while ATP synthesis stops.
claims.scope: The experimental demonstration that the stored quantity is a difference across a boundary, used to separate a compartment that is a container from a compartment that is a mechanism.
claims.uncertainty: The statement is about the effect on the proton potential and ATP synthesis in a laboratory setting. Nothing here concerns any use, dose, exposure or effect of these compounds in people, and the lesson makes no such statement.

claims.statement: Butyrate oxidation supplies 70 to 80 per cent of a mature colonocyte's energetic requirements; the butyrate is synthesised by resident bacteria in the lumen, and the colonocyte oxidises it to carbon dioxide through the mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation system.
claims.scope: The fuel a mature colonocyte actually runs on and where it comes from, used to connect the mitochondrial compartment to the bacterial population on the other side of the apical membrane.
claims.uncertainty: The 70 to 80 per cent figure describes mature colonocytes and does not describe the dividing cells at the crypt base, which have a different metabolism. The share will vary with diet, with the composition of the luminal community, and with the state of the tissue.

claims.statement: Mature colonocytes running mitochondrial beta-oxidation consume oxygen heavily through oxidative phosphorylation, and the resulting oxygen partial pressure at the epithelium is below 7.6 mmHg, under 1 per cent oxygen, a condition described as epithelial hypoxia.
claims.scope: The oxygen tension at the colonic epithelial surface and its origin in the metabolism of the epithelial cells themselves, used to show that a compartment's activity inside one cell has a consequence at tissue scale.
claims.uncertainty: The value is a reported figure for the healthy colonic epithelium and will vary with region, diet and disease. The lesson explicitly does not adopt the further claim that this hypoxia is what maintains the anaerobic luminal community, which is the review's own argument and an active research question.

claims.statement: Enterocytes of the intestinal lining are replaced every four to five days, while some other epithelial cell types in the same tissue persist far longer.
claims.scope: The replacement interval of the absorptive cell, carried forward from the first lesson of this block and used to show how often the delivery machinery has to rebuild a complete cell.
claims.uncertainty: This is a population-level interval, not a claim that every cell shares one lifetime. The same review notes that serotonin-producing enteroendocrine cells can persist for up to 28 days, so cell-type lifetimes within one crypt differ substantially.

claims.statement: Microvillus inclusion disease is caused by mutations in the genes for myosin Vb, syntaxin 3 or syntaxin binding protein 2, which produce a failure of vesicle trafficking or of the fusion of vesicles with the plasma membrane, with the result that vesicles containing apical proteins accumulate subapically.
claims.scope: The causal genes and the cellular mechanism of one intestinal epithelial polarity disorder, used as a worked case in which manufacture is intact and delivery fails.
claims.uncertainty: The reported gene set is not exhaustive and the review describes heterogeneous mutations with differing effects. Nothing here is a diagnostic criterion, a genotype-phenotype statement for any individual, or guidance for investigation or management.

claims.statement: Biopsies in microvillus inclusion disease show villus atrophy, absent or abnormal microvilli, subapical staining for a protein that belongs on the apical membrane, intracellular vesicle-like structures, and subapical microvillus inclusions.
claims.scope: The reported microscopic findings of one disorder, used to test whether the lesson's delivery model predicts what is actually seen.
claims.uncertainty: These are findings reported in a review of the condition, described in small-bowel tissue. The lesson states no sensitivity, specificity, frequency or diagnostic threshold for any of them and makes no statement about what any finding would mean in a real specimen.

claims.statement: Microvillus inclusion disease is a severe neonatal enteropathy that manifests mostly during the first days of life, with extremely watery diarrhoea, dehydration and weight loss.
claims.scope: The reported clinical presentation of one rare disorder, used only to check the lesson's prediction that a failure to build the absorptive surface produces a failure to absorb.
claims.uncertainty: This is a description of a reported presentation and not a diagnostic rule. Many conditions produce neonatal diarrhoea, and the lesson takes no position on how any real presentation should be interpreted, investigated or managed.

terms.definition: A space inside a cell enclosed by membrane, holding conditions that differ from the cytosol and actively maintained against the tendency of those differences to even out. The maintained part is what separates a compartment from a container: stop paying for the difference and it goes, while the membrane is still intact.

A compartment, or in a few cases a structure, with a recognisable identity and a job the others do not do, holding its own distinct set of proteins. Naming an organelle is the end of an explanation and not the beginning of one; the question that does the work is which maintained condition it holds.

The division of a cell's interior by membrane into separate compartments. It buys incompatible chemistries running at the same time, local concentrations unlike the cytosol, and a controlled sequence of operations imposed by a fixed order of compartments. It is charged for in membrane, in standing energy, in transport machinery and in an addressing system. It is the idea PREM-BIO-001 called emergence, applied one level below the tissue: the properties belong to the arrangement of parts and to no part alone.

The fluid inside a cell but outside its membrane-enclosed compartments, held near pH 7.2. It is the reference condition against which every compartment in this lesson is compared, and it is where a protein stays when nothing directs it elsewhere.

The absorptive cell of the colonic epithelium, and the kind of enterocyte that makes up most of that lining. It is polarised, with an apical surface meeting the lumen and a basolateral surface meeting neighbouring cells and the tissue beneath, and it is the running example of this lesson.

The face of an epithelial cell that meets the lumen. In a colonocyte it carries the brush border and is where uptake from the gut contents happens. Its protein complement differs from that of the basolateral surface, and a protein delivered to the wrong one of the two is in the wrong place.

The face of an epithelial cell away from the lumen: the base in contact with the material the sheet sits on, together with the sides in contact with neighbouring cells. In a colonocyte it is where absorbed material is handed onward towards the blood.

The dense array of fine projections, around a thousand of them on a mature absorptive cell, that covers the apical surface and multiplies the area available for uptake. Each projection is a microvillus. Under a light microscope the array reads as one fuzzy border, which is where the name comes from. A microvillus is one projection; the brush border is the array of them, so the two are not interchangeable.

A compartment held near pH 5 by a proton pump in its membrane, containing acid hydrolases that break down material taken into the cell and worn-out organelles. The acid interior is not a convenience for the enzymes. It is what switches them on, and therefore also what makes them safe for the cell to own.

A degradative enzyme whose activity is optimal in acid conditions, around pH 4.5 to 5.0 for the lysosomal set. The name records a requirement and not a location: the same enzyme at the cytosolic pH of about 7.2 can do little.

A compartment that runs oxidation reactions, including the breakdown of fatty acids too long for mitochondria to start on, and that carries catalase alongside the oxidases producing hydrogen peroxide, so the peroxide is destroyed where it is made. It segregates a reactive product, which is a different problem from the one the lysosome solves.

A membrane compartment reaching through much of the cell, held near pH 7.2, which receives proteins carrying a signal sequence while they are still being made and is where their folding begins. The rough form is the part studded with the ribosomes making those proteins.

A stack of compartments running from about pH 6.7 at the face receiving cargo from the endoplasmic reticulum to about 6.0 at the face dispatching it. Proteins are modified in a fixed order as they pass through, and the final compartment, the trans-Golgi network, sorts them by destination and packages them into transport vesicles.

A stretch of a newly made protein's own amino-acid sequence that says where the protein should go. The signal sequence for the endoplasmic reticulum is recognised by the signal recognition particle as it emerges from the ribosome, and that recognition diverts the whole ribosome and unfinished chain to the endoplasmic reticulum membrane.

The machinery that gets each product to the compartment or the cell face where it works: a destination encoded in the product, and a receptor able to read it. The mannose 6-phosphate group added to lysosomal enzymes in the Golgi, and recognised by mannose 6-phosphate receptors in the trans-Golgi network, is one complete example. Targeting can fail on its own, leaving a correctly made product in the wrong place.

A small membrane-bounded sac that carries cargo between compartments, or from the trans-Golgi network to a chosen face of the cell surface, and delivers it by fusing with the target membrane. Moving the vesicle and fusing it are separate steps, and they can fail separately.

A compartment whose boundary is part of its mechanism. The electron transport chain pumps protons across that boundary and the return flow of protons drives ATP synthase. Because a gradient is a difference between two sides, removing the boundary removes the device instead of merely opening it.

A difference in hydrogen-ion concentration between the two sides of a membrane, which is what the pH values in this lesson describe and what the arithmetic here computes. A membrane usually also carries a difference in charge, the membrane potential, and the two together make the proton-motive force, or proton electrochemical potential, which is the quantity that drives ATP synthase in the mitochondrion. The chemical and electrical parts are separable, and this lesson computes only the chemical one.

A short-chain fatty acid made by the bacteria of the colonic lumen from material the host has not digested. It supplies seventy to eighty per cent of a mature colonocyte's energy, oxidised inside that cell's mitochondria.

The third-party drawing is a reference that lets a learner attach names to places once; it is a generic animal cell with a flagellum and no apical or basolateral asymmetry, so the scene states plainly that it is not the lesson's case cell and that the argument is not organised around it.
